cl_nic_smoking_health.q: How much does smoking shorten life?
cl_nic_smoking_health.short: About 11 to 12 years on average, a big US study estimates. Of 100 women who smoked, 38 would reach 80, against 70 who never smoked.
cl_nic_smoking_health.but: These are averages for groups in one US study, not a forecast for any one person. It looked at cigarettes only.
how: About 202,000 US adults aged 25 or older were interviewed in 1997 to 2004 and followed through death records for about 7 years. At ages 25 to 79, people who smoked died at about 3 times the rate of people who never smoked (under 100 cigarettes in their lives).

The gap was biggest for lung cancer, at about 15 to 18 times the rate, and other lung and breathing diseases, about 8 to 9 times. For heart disease it was about 3 times. The authors estimate that about 6 in 10 deaths among people who smoked at these ages wouldn't have happened at the disease death rates of people who never smoked.

Scaled to US death rates in 2004, 38 in 100 women and 26 in 100 men who smoked would live from 25 to 80, against 70 and 61 in 100 who never smoked. A 2014 US Surgeon General's report judges that smoking raises the risk of dying and causes disease in nearly every organ.

Compared with people who kept smoking, people who had stopped gained roughly 10 years if they stopped at 25 to 34, 9 at 35 to 44, 6 at 45 to 54 and 4 at 55 to 64. Those who stopped around 40 still died at 1.2 times the rate of people who never smoked, against 3 times for those who kept on.
cl_nic_smoking_health.rate: One large nationwide study, linked to death records. It didn't account for diet, exercise or income, but those are unlikely to explain a threefold gap. The figures on stopping are rougher.

cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.q: Is it the nicotine or the smoke that does the harm?
cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.short: Burned tobacco causes most of tobacco's harm, a big US report says. But it judges that nicotine on its own can still harm an unborn baby.
cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.but: It doesn't say how much of smoking's harm comes from nicotine itself. And the report sums up other studies, so this is second-hand.
how: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report says burned tobacco, like cigarettes, causes by far most of tobacco's death and disease in the US. That's about products. It doesn't split the harm between nicotine and the rest of the smoke.

For nicotine alone, it found enough evidence that it can poison in high enough amounts. It also judged that nicotine harms an unborn baby's growing brain and adds to early births and stillbirths. The brain finding comes from lab studies, the pregnancy one mostly from smokeless tobacco and patch trials.

For teenagers' brains, it called the evidence suggestive but not enough. For cancer, it was too thin to say either way. It made no ruling on the heart, but calls it likely that nicotine adds somewhat to heart risk in people who smoke.

It says nicotine is the main thing in tobacco that hooks people, but nicotine medicines carry a low risk of that. In adults, even some who don't smoke, nicotine gave a small boost to thinking. Authors paid by tobacco firms reported almost only good effects on thinking.
cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.rate: One big US government report that sums up other studies and doesn't say how it found them. For nicotine on its own, it leans on animal studies and other products, not on people using nicotine alone.

cl_nic_smoke_nearby.short: Yes, two big US reports judge. It's linked to sudden infant death and asthma, and to 20 to 30% more lung cancer in adults who don't smoke.
cl_nic_smoke_nearby.but: These are the reports' judgments of other studies, so the figures are second-hand. And the later report builds on the earlier one.
how: In children, the 2006 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence that others' smoke causes sudden infant death. The same went for chest and ear illness, wheeze, asthma at school age, weaker lungs and a small drop in birth weight. For early birth and some childhood cancers, the evidence was suggestive but not enough.

In adults who don't smoke, it found enough evidence for lung cancer and heart disease. Living with someone who smokes went with a 20 to 30% higher lung cancer risk, and heart disease risk was 25 to 30% higher.
The 2014 report added stroke, with a risk about 20 to 30% higher. It also found that smoke-free laws were followed by fewer heart attacks and similar events in people under 65.

The 2006 report says no level of secondhand smoke is risk-free. The parts we read give no figures for that, and by our reading it rests mostly on lab findings. The report expects less cancer risk than from smoking, since people breathe in far less of the cancer-causing chemicals.
cl_nic_smoke_nearby.rate: Two US government reports that sum up other studies, and the later builds on the earlier. We saw only their summaries, which is why the evidence counts as very limited here, not because the reports doubted the links.

nicotine.statement: Quitting smoking after 55 is too late to make any difference.
nicotine.why: In a big US study, people who stopped at 55 to 64 gained roughly 4 years compared with people who kept smoking. That's a group average.

nicotine.statement: Quitting smoking by 40 wipes out all the extra risk of dying early.
nicotine.why: In a big US study, people who stopped around 40 still died at 1.2 times the rate of people who never smoked, against 3 times for those who kept smoking.

nicotine.statement: Nicotine gum and patches hook people as much as smoking does.
nicotine.why: A big US report says nicotine medicines carry a low risk of getting hooked. That's the report's judgment of other studies.

nicotine.statement: It's been proven that nicotine on its own causes cancer.
nicotine.why: A big US report found the evidence too thin to say either way. It says burned tobacco causes most of tobacco's harm.

nicotine.statement: Breathing other people's smoke has been linked to sudden infant death.
nicotine.why: A 2006 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence to call it a cause. That's the report's judgment of other studies.

nicotine.statement: After smoke-free laws came in, heart attacks fell in people under 65.
nicotine.why: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence for fewer heart attacks and similar events in people under 65. That's the report's judgment, second-hand.
